title: The Glasshouse of the family house on Kessler Street
premise: Zephyrine Underhill, a restaurant critic who lost her sense of taste after the fire that reshaped her family, returns to Kessler Street for her grandmother's funeral and discovers a stranger mourning under the name 'Glasshouse'—a name the family buried decades ago. As she pieces together why her relatives arranged their lives around silence, she learns the fire was no accident and that her own survival was bought with someone else's erasure. The last bus route to the old neighborhood is being permanently rerouted, forcing her to choose between protecting the family's fiction and speaking the truth aloud. In the end, she testifies to what really happened, loses several family members but gains an honest one in the stranger—who turns out to be the daughter of the man the family let take the blame—and tastes food again for the first time in five years.
about_author: Zephyrine Ishikawa is the pen name of a former line cook turned essayist who writes about memory, appetite, and the families we construct around our silences. She lives above a shuttered diner and insists she can still smell everything.

chapters.title: The Almost-Said
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. At a tasting menu she cannot taste, Zephyrine drafts a review full of beautiful evasions, establishing her five-year practice of 'almost saying it.' A phone call summons her home for her grandmother Vera's funeral. Emotional beat: numb competence cracking at the edges as the past pulls.

chapters.title: Kessler Street, Rerouted
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She arrives to find the old neighborhood half-demolished and learns the last bus route will be cut within weeks—a ticking clock. Her siblings greet her with rehearsed warmth. Emotional beat: the uncanny feeling of returning to a stage set where everyone knows their lines except her.

chapters.title: A Stranger Named Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. At the wake, a woman signs the guest book 'Mara Glasshouse,' a name nobody uses. When Zephyrine asks, her brother Daniel goes white and her aunt changes the subject with practiced grace. Emotional beat: first fracture—the family's choreography visibly failing for the first time.

chapters.title: What Vera Kept
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Zephyrine and Mara. Zephyrine searches Vera's locked glasshouse conservatory and finds a scorched ledger; Mara, watching from outside, leaves a note asking to talk. Emotional beat: curiosity hardening into resolve, and the first hint that Mara has been waiting years for this door to open.

chapters.title: The Fire, Version One
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. Daniel recounts the official story—the 1998 blaze, the handyman Tomás convicted of arson—to Zephyrine over drinks, too smoothly. Flashbacks show him coaching his children on what not to say. Emotional beat: loyalty portrayed as love, but the seams of rehearsal showing through.

chapters.title: Tomás's Daughter
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara tells Zephyrine her side: her father died in prison insisting he was paid to confess, and Vera sent anonymous money until two years ago. She shows Zephyrine the money orders signed with a familiar initial. Emotional beat: grief meeting grief—two daughters of the same lie recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Version Two
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Cross-referencing the ledger and Vera's letters, Zephyrine reconstructs the truth: Uncle Alden started the fire for insurance, and the family let Tomás hang to protect him—and to protect Zephyrine, then a child hiding in the glasshouse. Emotional beat: vertigo; her taste-loss reframed as survivor's guilt made physical.

chapters.title: The Family Arrangement
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge at an emergency dinner. Aunt Ruth admits it; Daniel threatens disownment; cousin Priya quietly sides with Zephyrine. The question surfaces: was protecting Zephyrine worth destroying Tomás? Emotional beat: open war—loyalty and truth finally forced into the same room.

chapters.title: Last Bus to Kessler Street
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. On the final run of the old bus route, Zephyrine rides to the ruins with Mara and publicly reads Vera's confession letter at the site, before neighbors and Daniel both. Emotional beat: climax—she says it, fully, for the first time, and the cost lands immediately.

chapters.title: Salt, Then Sweet
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, months later. Some family is gone; Priya remains; Mara becomes something like a sister. In a small diner near the rerouted stop, Zephyrine writes a review that names everything plainly—and mid-sentence, tastes her soup. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; truth costs, but it restores appetite.
